A day later it had recovered almost all of the loss. Alerts like this one appear daily, and markets can react to them quickly. A few simple checks show how much an alert actually tells you. Understand what trackers can see, and what they can't Every transfer on a public blockchain such as Ethereum is visible: which address sent coins, which address received them, how many, and when. Analytics platforms such as Arkham Intelligence and services such as Lookonchain turn that data into readable alerts. Trackers can't see who owns an address unless it has been identified, and they can't see what happens inside an exchange. Once coins reach an exchange deposit address, any sale happens on the exchange's internal order book, which is not recorded on the blockchain. title: How Singapore's monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
body: How Singapore's monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers Most central banks fight inflation by raising or cutting interest rates. Singapore does it differently. The Monetary Authority of Singapore steers the economy by managing the value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners' currencies. When MAS "tightens," it lets the currency strengthen faster, which makes imports cheaper and cools inflation. When it "eases," it slows or reverses that appreciation. That is why Wednesday's decision to hold policy steady was framed entirely in terms of an exchange rate band, with no mention of an interest rate. Why Singapore uses the exchange rate Singapore is one of the most open economies in the world. It imports most of what it consumes, from food and fuel to raw materials, and trade flows are large relative to the size of its economy. That makes the exchange rate a far more powerful influence on prices than domestic interest rates. There is also a practical constraint. Singapore allows capital to move freely in and out of the country. A central bank with open capital flows can control either its exchange rate or its interest rates, but not both. MAS chose the exchange rate in 1981, and local interest rates largely follow global rates, particularly those in the US. What is the S$NEER?

Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility.

This was the highest rate since June, driven primarily by faster non-food inflation (1.5% vs 1.2% in August). The main contributor was a sharper rise in transport costs (4.3% vs 2.5%), reflecting higher fuel prices and stronger travel demand ahead of the Golden Week holidays. Additional upward pressure came from clothing (1.2% vs 1.3%), healthcare (2.7% vs 2.7%), and education (1.4% vs 1.4%). By contrast, housing costs remained weak, registering a decline of 0.3% for the second consecutive month (-0.3% vs -0.3%). Food prices fell for the sixth consecutive month (-1.7% vs -1.4%), led by a further drop in pork prices, as abundant supply and subdued consumption continued to drag on the market. On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.2%, undershooting forecasts of a 0.3% rise and easing from August's 0.4% gain, which had been the strongest monthly increase since February. title: Connecting the dots: Why strong US bank earnings don't always mean a healthy economy
body: Earnings season is upon us again. And as is usually the case, Wall Street's biggest banks are the ones to get the ball rolling as they did yesterday. We had the likes of JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Citi and Wells Fargo report their latest quarterly results and it was a mixed bag to say the least. Goldman Sachs and Citi delivered solid earnings beats, while JP Morgan disappointed with a rare earnings miss. Meanwhile, Wells Fargo fell short on revenue expectations, despite reporting better-than-expected profits. Having said that, we're still talking about some of the biggest banks in the world making billions of dollars in profits every quarter regardless. So, that surely must mean the US economy is doing pretty well, no? Well, not necessarily. Just because the big banks are making billions doesn't mean that the rest of the economy is thriving just as much. And to understand why that is the case, we need to look at how banks actually make their money. Let's take an example where I am the bank. I will take deposits from my customers, pay them interest and then lend that money to someone else at a higher interest rate. Assuming I pay my depositors 2% interest and charge my borrowers 7% interest, that's a 5% difference before accounting for all the other costs. That doesn't seem too shabby, no? Well, that is essentially how banks earn their money from lending.

title: Spain September CPI confirmed at 4.9% as rising core inflation adds to ECB rate hike pressure
body: Spain September final CPI +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y prelim Prior +4.3% Spain September final HICP +5.0% vs +5.0% y/y prelim Prior +4.6% Spain September core CPI +3.1% y/y Prior +2.9% The final report confirms another uncomfortable rise in Spanish inflation in September, with headline annual inflation rising to 4.9% from 4.3% in August. The harmonised reading also jumps further to clip the 5% mark, the highest since February 2023. The main culprit is of course the surge in energy prices, largely stemming from the Middle East conflict. But when looking at core prices, that is where the latest Spanish figures become a little more troubling. Core annual inflation climbed to 3.1% in September from 2.9% previously. And that is the highest level since March 2024. While the ECB can afford to look past temporary energy shocks, the concern is when those higher costs start filtering through to other goods and services. And with core prices starting to move up now, there are growing risks that the initial price shock is starting to feed into broader inflation pressures. In turn, that means making the eventual return to its 2% target a much more difficult task. Now, this is just one report and it won't be enough on its own to force the ECB into another rate hike. But with the ECB already having raised interest rates twice already this summer, the latest data certainly makes the argument for staying cautious a little stronger.

title: German wholesale prices continue to push higher in September, keeping inflation risks in focus

That marks the highest annual price jump since February 2023 and will add to inflation concerns in the German economy. Much of the price jump this year can be attributed to the Middle East conflict, which resulted in higher wholesale prices of energy products and intermediate goods such as metals, in particular. Looking at the details, the main cause of the annual increase in wholesale prices is tied to the increase in the prices of mineral oil products, with prices up 48.8% from September 2025. Compared with August 2026, prices rose by 10.5%. Meanwhile, the increase in prices in the wholesale of non-ferrous ores, non-ferrous metals and non-ferrous semi-finished metal products (+24.9% on September 2025, +2.1% on August 2026) also had a considerable impact on the development of prices compared with the same month of the previous year. Overall, the latest reading here continues to paint a rather uncomfortable picture for Germany as businesses continue to face rising input costs. And with energy prices being a major contributor, there is only so much that firms can do to absorb those increases before passing some of the burden on to consumers.

title: Economic data spotlight: Will the US CPI report change the Fed's rate hike plans?
body: There's a lot riding on the US CPI report later today, especially with Treasury yields having threatened multi-decade highs over the past week. Going into the report, the consensus is that headline inflation is going to look rather ugly. The question now though is whether markets will actually care all that much. Headline inflation is expected to rise by 0.6% on the month, taking the annual estimate to 3.6%. It is anticipated that much of the rise will be driven by higher gasoline prices amid the ongoing tensions in the Middle East. Looking to core inflation, that is expected to rise by a more modest 0.2% on the month and 2.5% annually. Now, the Fed can arguably afford to look past a temporary spike in energy prices. And that is something I would expect policymakers to do in reacting to this report. But if those price pressures start filtering through to other parts of the economy, that is where the story starts becoming something different altogether. As such, the main focus should really be on core prices today - alongside the details such as shelter costs and services inflation. A surprise there would suggest that underlying price pressures are proving stickier than the Fed might like. As for the bond market, the reaction there could be telling for how broader markets might react to the inflation numbers. A hotter headline figure accompanied by a relatively benign core reading might actually give Treasury yields some room to retreat.

title: What are the key levels in play for the US dollar after the hotter than expected CPI
body: The US CPI came in higher than expectations and that has stocks lower, yields higher, and the dollar moving to the upside. Where are the problem areas? Energy is the immediate problem. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in September, following 3.9% in August. Fuel oil rose 15.3%, following 10.1%. Energy's June and July declines have given way to substantial increases. Electricity and piped gas were much more contained in September. Services inflation is becoming firmer. Services excluding energy progressed from +0.2% in July to +0.3% in August and +0.4% in September. That steady acceleration is a concern because it suggests the underlying pressure is broader than volatile energy prices. Shelter has picked up again. Monthly increases moved from +0.1% in June and July to +0.3% in August and +0.4% in September. Its three-month average remains below the six-month average, so the longer comparison still shows improvement. The latest monthly direction, however, is less encouraging. Transportation services show a clear reversal. After declines in May and June, prices increased 0.3%, 0.5%, and 0.6% over July–September. Energy prices are leading over into all goods that have to be transported that higher energy prices. This isn't rocket science. Core goods are providing less relief. Their three-month average is roughly three times the six-month average. Used vehicles stand out: +0.4% in July, +0.4% in August, and +0.7% in September.

title: S&P 500 technical analysis after the CPI selloff
body: S&P 500 futures: CPI selloff threatens the recovery channel, with a lower support test in view S&P 500 E-mini futures have turned lower following the US CPI report, with the four-hour chart showing a potentially important deterioration in the short-term technical picture. About half an hour before the US cash market opens, futures are trading near 7,828, having fallen sharply from the 7,870 area. Let's jump into my simple 4h chart S&P 500 futures chart: Three observations stand out. 1. The earlier breakout was meaningful, but its momentum has faded. After approximately five attempts, S&P 500 futures finally broke above the descending purple resistance line in early October. That breakout was subsequently tested around October 8-9, when price briefly pierced the former resistance before recovering. This was constructive behavior. A previously troublesome resistance area appeared to be taking on a supporting role. However, the subsequent rally stalled below the October 6 high near 7,897, leaving a lower high. The recovery was therefore losing some of its strength even before today's decline. 2. The rising channel has broken, potentially activating a bear flag. The pitchfork drawn over the latest recovery also functions as a rising price channel. Following the sharp decline from the October 6 high, the subsequent advance took place within this upward-sloping structure. That creates the possibility of a bear flag: a temporary recovery within a developing downward move.

title: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
body: The stakes around the October Federal Reserve meeting suddenly got much higher. Today's US CPI report was hot across the board, including in core measures that are less volatile than the energy-driven headline. The bond market quickly repriced on the data, with US 2-year yields now up 15 basis points on the day to 4.94%. In the Fed funds futures market, pricing is now right at 50/50 for a hike or hold this month. It's also critical to note that the Fed goes into the blackout period on Saturday. That leaves just three days to shape the narrative if the Fed doesn't want to go into the meeting with raised stakes. That starts today with a 1:30 pm ET speech from Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin. I'm a fan of Barkin's level-headed style and he usually represents the core views of the Fed, so that's one to watch especially closely. That said, we just heard from Barkin this week and he didn't offer much in the way of guidance. One notable recent comment from him was in late September when he said that this cycle could be like the 1990s mid-cycle adjustment. Barkin was comparing now to an easing cycle in the 1990s, when Greenspan cut rates by 75 bps over seven months at the end of 1995. So by that analogue -- if you took it directly -- would be more dovish than what is priced in now. He also said he would not yet make an overheating case, but economy is firming and not weakening and that businesses feel they have pricing power.

title: How to identify the economic data that really moves markets
body: One of the biggest challenges for new traders is knowing which economic releases deserve the most attention. Economic calendars typically classify indicators as low, medium or high impact, but these labels can be misleading. A release marked as high impact can sometimes pass without moving markets much, while a low impact indicator can trigger a significant reaction. The impact of economic data depends not only on the indicator itself, but also on the current economic environment, central bank focus and what the market has already priced in. Why impact ratings on calendars are useless Economic calendars generally assign impact ratings based on how much volatility an indicator has historically generated. However, historical volatility does not account for current context. For example, US CPI is usually considered a high impact release because inflation plays a major role in the Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions. But if inflation has been broadly stable and the Fed has made it clear that it is more concerned about the labour market, the same inflation report might generate a relatively muted reaction. Conversely, a weaker than expected employment report could trigger a significant market move if traders are increasingly concerned about a deteriorating labour market and are looking for confirmation that the Fed will cut rates. This is why traders should avoid relying exclusively on economic calendar labels.

title: China's September lending surprise masks a much deeper slump in credit demand
body: China's new bank loans climbed to ¥1.08 trillion in September, beating market expectations of ¥975 billion. At first glance, that seems like a welcome improvement especially after the rather dismal lending figures we've seen over the past few months. That being said, lending is still down roughly 16% compared to September last year. And adding to that, the year-on-date snapshot isn't pretty either. In looking at the first nine months of 2026, Chinese banks have now extended ¥11.52 trillion in new loans during this period. That falls short when viewed in comparison to the ¥14.75 trillion over the same period last year. In short, we're looking at a rather substantial 22% decline in new lending this year. I would argue that the figures above tell us quite a bit about the state of China's domestic economy. The problem that China is facing right now is not that banks aren't willing to lend. It is more of a case that households and businesses aren't particularly eager to borrow in the first place. A big part of that can be traced back to the property market crash that unfolded in 2021. With the property sector still struggling to this day, households have little incentive to take on new mortgages. Meanwhile, businesses aren't exactly rushing to expand operations when domestic consumption remains sluggish.

title: Bitcoin sellers defend moving average resistance. What does that teach traders?
body: US stocks are lower, Treasury yields are higher, and oil prices are higher. That risk-off backdrop is weighing on Bitcoin. But for traders, the technical levels help answer the more practical questions: Who has control? Where is the risk? What needs to happen next? The moving average gives traders a decision point On the four-hour chart, Bitcoin fell below its 100-bar moving average on October 7. After finding support near $80,106 on October 8, the price rebounded but stalled against that moving average on October 12 and again today. Why does that matter? A moving average can act as support when the price is above it and resistance when the price is below it. In this case, the rebounds more recently in Bitcoin gave buyers opportunities to reclaim the 200 and the 100 bar moving averages on the 4-hour chart. The 200 bar MA (green line), was broken but sellers leaned near the 100 bar MA (blue line). Buyers could not get and stay above the higher MA. Sellers leaned against the level and pushed the price back lower. The buyers had their shot. They missed. For sellers, that moving average provides a reference point to define risk. Stay below keeps the bearish bias intact. Move above and stay above, and the reason for leaning against that resistance begins to weaken. The moving average does not guarantee the next move. It gives traders a level against which to judge the price action.

title: Canadian dollar touches an 18-month low as the US dollar jumps on hot CPI

The 70-cent level is a sensitive one domestically and a clean break of it could give Canadians another reason not to travel south this winter. The loonie had made strong gains yesterday as the post-jobs report weakness reversed. Friday's data saw Canada unexpectedly shed jobs but a closer look showed it was driven by government job losses in healthcare and education. The latter is a category that's particularly hard to seasonally adjust for in September due to school restarting while neither is indicative of underlying economic strength. That said, there have been mixed indications on the Canadian economy and the housing sector in much of the country appears to be in the midst of another leg down. Where it gets interesting is how central banks are reacting. In the year ahead, there are 97 basis points of hikes priced in for the Bank of Canada and 92 basis points for the Federal Reserve. Today's US CPI report narrowed that gap and if we see the Canadian economy stumble or the US accelerate further, then a real USD-positive divergence could open up. title: Fed's Daly: more rate hikes likely needed, but no urgency to move in October
body: Daly's comments are the clearest pushback yet against the jump in October hike pricing that followed the CPI data. Expect them to trim the odds of a move on October 27-28 without denting expectations for a December increase. That mix would ease some pressure on the front end of the Treasury curve while leaving longer-dated yields anchored to a higher-for-longer outlook. Because Daly linked headline inflation directly to gasoline prices, oil remains the key swing factor. A further surge in crude tied to the Iran war would test her view that the Fed can afford to wait. Her remarks also contrast with Goolsbee's more anxious tone, a reminder that officials agree on direction but not on timing. --- Daly agrees the Fed probably has more hiking to do, but she sees no reason to rush it out the door this month.

title: Fed catch up - Goolsbee calls CPI discouraging as Beige Book flags diesel-fuelled price pressure
body: Together, the two releases make an October hike harder to dismiss. Markets are pricing close to a 40% chance of a move on October 27-28, even though key officials had steered expectations toward December. The oil link is central: diesel costs from the Iran war now run through freight, farming and airfares, which raises the risk of second-round effects the Fed cannot easily look through. That supports Treasury yields at the front end and the US dollar, and keeps mortgage rates under upward pressure. Further strength in crude or diesel would add weight to the case for moving sooner. Next week's Fed commentary, before the pre-meeting blackout, is the next test of whether officials push back on October pricing. --- One Fed president is hearing about prices everywhere he goes, and the Fed's own survey says businesses are hearing about diesel even more.

title: 10-Year T-Note futures bounce off contract lows as market digests hot CPI data.
body: Treasury markets experienced a volatile session on Wednesday following a hotter-than-expected CPI print. The 10-Year T-Note futures initially faced selling pressure, dropping to an intraday low of 103'29—some of the lowest levels for the contract—before reversing course. Prices rallied a full point to trade near 104'29, notching a second consecutive session of upward momentum. Market participants seemingly looked past the inflation data, with sentiment suggesting the Fed will still pause in October. The yield curve flattened as divergent price action took hold. While front-end yields saw selling pressure from the CPI release, the back end of the curve attracted buyers. The 10-Year yield dropped more than 3 bps to 4.18%, falling 15 bps off its intraday high of 4.33%, aided in part by spillover buying pressure from a selloff in equities.

title: E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures drop as hot CPI data pressures tech.
body: Equity index futures faced heavy selling pressure on Wednesday, with E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures leading the decline. The tech-heavy contract posted its largest percentage drop since July 23, falling about 4.5% from its all-time high amid a broader market pullback. Hotter-than-expected September inflation data served as the primary catalyst. Headline CPI rose 3.7% year-over-year, while core inflation climbed 2.6% annually—the fastest monthly pace since April. The strong data pushed the probability of an October Fed rate hike from 22% to 32%, driving Treasury yields higher and weighing heavily on growth-sensitive tech valuations. Semiconductor weakness amplified the selling after a major chip equipment manufacturer missed quarterly revenue estimates despite raising its 2026 outlook.

title: Soybean futures trade sideways as harvest pace dictates direction.
body: Agricultural futures saw mixed trading action on Wednesday as traders digested a blend of fundamental data and harvest progress. Soybean futures traded in a choppy 19'2-cent range, initially finding support from a 10-cargo Chinese purchase before facing heavy selling pressure that left the market mostly sideways. Option open interest is clearing out with only days left in the November contract, and soybean CVOL sits at 13.8%. Corn futures felt pressure from mixed fundamentals, with the harvest advancing 10% but still trailing the average pace by 6%. While inspections rose 5% year-over-year, exports dropped 4%, keeping the December contract churning in a tight range before settling lower. Wheat futures navigated a choppy session, bouncing off one-month lows as winter wheat planting reached 51%, keeping progress 7% behind the historical average. The Chicago December contract recovered from early lows to post modest gains.

title: Lean Hog Futures Hit Contract Low on Shifting Consumer Demand
